implementation_notes: Kotlin's extension functions are the natural destination when the data class is in code you do not own or cannot modify, and they also make the envy visible at the call site. They are still a partial cure: the knowledge lives outside the type. Prefer moving the function into the class when you own it; use an extension when you do not. Kotlin's data classes and `copy()` make it easy to end up with rule-shaped code that constructs new instances of other people's types — which is envy with a type-safety problem attached.
idiom_name: extension function on the wrong receiver
pitfalls: Extension functions are picked by import scope, so two files can define incompatible `label()` extensions and the conflict only appears at the call site.
A receiver-typed `val Order.something` property reads as if it were state but is computed on every access.
Scope functions (`also`, `run`) inside a method can make the envy invisible to both readers and linters.
